insider_note: This is the mirror image of ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁵x/(sin⁵x + cos⁵x) dx — swap sin and cos throughout and the same King's-property method gives the same final value, π/4, so the two integrals are equal by symmetry.

steps.label: Apply the property with a = π/2
steps.margin_note: One mark. Label the given integral (1).
steps.memory_tip: This is the sin/cos mirror of ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁵x/(sin⁵x + cos⁵x) dx — the same method applies with the roles reversed.
steps.why: Labelling the given integral (1) sets it up for comparison with its transformed second form.
common_mistakes: Not stating the property line before applying it.
Confusing this integral with the version whose numerator is sin⁵x.

steps.label: Write the second form
steps.margin_note: One more mark. cos⁵x turns into sin⁵x under the swap.
steps.memory_tip: cos(π/2 − x) = sinx, so cos⁵(π/2 − x) = sin⁵x.
steps.why: Under x → π/2 − x, cosx becomes sinx, so cos⁵x becomes sin⁵x in the numerator, while the denominator (a sum of both powers) reappears unchanged.
common_mistakes: Leaving the numerator as cos⁵x instead of turning it into sin⁵x.
Writing the denominator's two terms in a different order and treating it as a different quantity.

steps.label: Add and solve
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Adding (1) and (2) makes the integrand 1, so 2J is just the length of the interval.
steps.memory_tip: cos⁵x + sin⁵x over sin⁵x + cos⁵x is always 1 — the numerator sum always matches the denominator after this swap.
steps.why: The added numerator matches the denominator exactly, so the integrand equals 1 for every x, reducing the integral to the length of the interval, π/2.
common_mistakes: Reporting a value other than π/4 instead of noticing that 2J = π/2.
Forgetting to divide by 2 at the end.
